common_name: White Mischief Mexican Bush Sage (All-White Velvet Sage)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; White Mischief is an all-white-flowered sport of Mexican bush sage that keeps blooming later into the cool season than the purple forms in mild Gulf Coast winters.

directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings or container plants in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, giving this vigorous selection plenty of room since it can mound out much wider than tall in a single warm season. White Mischief is an all-white sport of Mexican bush sage: unlike the species and most named forms, both the fuzzy calyx and the small tubular flower are pure white rather than purple, giving long, wand-like flower spikes a softer, moonlit look against the same felted gray-green foliage. It flowers from late summer into winter in zone 9-11, often continuing later into the cool season than purple-flowered relatives, and it is just as attractive to late-season hummingbirds and butterflies. Cut the whole plant back hard, to roughly a foot, after a killing freeze knocks the top growth down, and expect vigorous regrowth from the woody crown the following spring.

common_name: Danielle's Dream Mexican Bush Sage (Pink Velvet Sage)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Danielle's Dream carries soft pink flowers within downy white calyxes rather than the purple-and-white spikes of the species, and it reblooms more continuously through the warm season before peaking in fall.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; this pastel selection of Mexican bush sage was patented as 'Ferpink' and is sold under the trade name Danielle's Dream. Instead of the deep purple calyx typical of the species, the fuzzy bracts are a soft downy white that cradles rosy-pink true flowers, producing long arching spikes with a gentler, two-tone pastel effect rather than the bold purple-and-white contrast of the standard form. It reblooms over a longer stretch of the growing season than many Mexican bush sage selections, with a strong flush in spring and summer in addition to the typical fall peak, and it draws hummingbirds and pollinators throughout. Like other Mexican bush sage forms, it is deer- and rabbit-resistant and drought-tolerant once established; cut the woody framework back to about a foot after winter dieback to renew the plant each spring.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs after the last frost in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Firefly is a fine-textured firebush selection with leaves and flowers about half the size of the species, giving a denser, more refined look than Compacta or the standard species.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Firefly is a scaled-down selection of the native firebush distinguished by proportionally smaller leaves and flowers than either the straight species or the popular 'Compacta' cultivar, giving the shrub a finer, denser texture while still producing the same orange-red tubular flowers almost continuously from late spring through frost. The smaller flower clusters open in greater numbers along the stems, so bloom coverage stays heavy even though individual flowers are more modest in size, and the foliage takes on bronze-orange tones as nights cool in fall. Hummingbirds and butterflies, especially gulf fritillary and swallowtails, visit the flowers throughout the warm season, and the dark berries that follow feed songbirds into winter. In zone 9, expect Firefly to die back to the root crown after a hard freeze and resprout vigorously in spring; cut the frozen stems back to 6-12 inches once new growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to shade after nights stay reliably warm; Wooly Strobilanthes is grown chiefly for its dense, silvery-haired foliage rather than its small purple flowers, and it tolerates salt spray and coastal wind better than most silver-leaved plants.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to shade -- this South Indian and Sri Lankan hill-country shrub is unusually adaptable across the light spectrum for a silver-foliage plant. Every leaf of Wooly Strobilanthes is coated in dense, cottony silver-gray hairs (gossypinus means cotton-like) that catch the light with a shimmering, pewter-metallic glow, giving the mounded, arching shrub year-round textural interest independent of bloom. Small tubular purple flowers appear in late summer into fall but are secondary to the foliage display. The woolly leaf surface sheds salt spray and drying wind unusually well for the genus, making this an option for exposed coastal beds and large containers where Persian shield's thinner leaves would scorch. In zone 9, protect from hard freezes or grow as a container specimen brought under cover in winter; pinch tips periodically to keep the mound dense.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or plant rooted cuttings and divisions in spring in light, fertile, free-draining soil in full sun to part shade; unlike its tender tropical cousin Persian shield, this Himalayan species tolerates hard freezes and can be left in the ground year-round well north of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant in light, fertile, free-draining soil in full sun to part shade, mulching the crown in winter in the colder end of its range. Strobilanthes wallichii is a Himalayan relative of showy Persian shield, but it is grown for cold hardiness and flowers rather than iridescent foliage -- the plain green, serrated leaves stay modest all season, and the show comes in late summer when curved, tubular purple-blue flowers open singly or in pairs along the upper stems. Its woody base and slowly creeping roots let it persist through winters that would kill tender Strobilanthes species outright, dying back to the crown in hard freezes and resprouting reliably in spring. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it can be treated as a true perennial rather than a replant-every-year tender plant, giving late-season blue-purple flower color to the partly shaded border when many summer bloomers are fading. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor.
